Sakshi Gupta, Jatin Rana 
Department of Electrical Engineering 
J.C. Bose University of Science and Technology, YMCA, Faridabad, India 
Corresponding author: sakshiguptaa411@gmail.com 
 
Abstract 
 
Electrooculography (EOG) provides a non-invasive means of measuring electrical changes associated with eye movements and blinking, 
making it useful for hands-free human–computer interaction. This work presents the design and evaluation of a low-cost EOG-based interface 
that recognizes a small set of ocular actions and converts them into real-time computer commands. The acquisition system uses a BioAmp 
EXG Pill connected to an ESP32 microcontroller, with electrodes positioned above and below the right eye for vertical EOG recording. 
Signals are sampled at 500 Hz and processed through embedded baseline and frequency filtering before transmission to a computer. 
The collected dataset contains 64,000 EOG samples organized into 160 trials, with 40 trials each for neutral gaze, upward eye movement, 
downward eye movement, and blinking. 
The original implementation produced 89.27% five-fold cross-validation accuracy and 91.14% hold-out accuracy after generating heavily 
overlapping windows. Because this evaluation can place strongly correlated windows in both training and test sets, an additional trial-level re-
analysis was performed using the original 160 trials as independent evaluation units.  
The selected EOG classes were also integrated into a real-time prototype in which upward and downward movements control vertical cursor 
motion and a double blink generates a mouse click. The results demonstrate the feasibility of a low-cost machine-learning-based EOG 
interaction pipeline while also showing the importance of trial-independent evaluation.

1.2 Literature Review 
Electrooculography (EOG) records small electrical potential 
changes produced by the eye’s movement and blinking. These 
signals are detected using electrodes placed around the eyes and 
can be analyzed to distinguish different eye activities. This 
capability makes EOG a useful input method for hands-free 
computer control, particularly in applications where conventional 
devices such as a mouse or keyboard may be difficult to use. 
Existing EOG systems have approached this problem in different 
ways. Ang et al. [2015] demonstrated a wearable single-channel 
EOG interface in which double-blink patterns were translated into 
cursor operations. Martínez-Cerveró et al. [2020] developed an 
open software/hardware EOG platform for classifying directional 
eye movements using conventional signal processing and 
machine learning. More recently, Hernández Pérez et al. [2023]

Electrooculography for Human–Computer Interaction 
Electrooculography records electrical variations associated with 
movement of the eye. The eye can be approximated electrically as 
a dipole in which the corneal region is relatively positive with 
respect to the retinal region. Movement of this dipole changes the 
voltage recorded by electrodes around the eyes [Chang, 2019]. 
The placement of electrodes depends on the movement of 
interest. Electrodes positioned on opposite horizontal sides of the 
eyes are commonly used for horizontal movement, whereas 
electrodes positioned above and below an eye can capture vertical 
movement. Blinking also produces a characteristic transient in 
vertical EOG because movement of the eyelid and ocular 
structures substantially affects the measured potential. 
Chang [2019] reviewed the use of EOG for HCI and described 
applications involving computer interaction, communication, 
mobility systems, and assistive interfaces. Belkhiria et al. [2022] 
subsequently reviewed EOG-based HCI work published between 
2000 and 2020, organizing such systems around stages including 
acquisition, processing, translation algorithms, and interaction 
commands. 
These observations motivate the architecture used in the present 
work: the physiological signal is first acquired and conditioned, 
transformed into quantitative descriptors, classified into a small 
action vocabulary, and finally passed through a decision layer 
before an operating-system command is executed. 
EOG Cursor-Control Systems 
Cursor interaction has been a recurring application of EOG 
because directional eye movements and blinking can naturally be 
mapped to navigation and selection operations. 
Ang et al. [2015] proposed a wearable single-channel system 
based on double-blink EOG activity. Their implementation 
demonstrated that a small ocular command vocabulary can be 
used to control cursor navigation and actions without requiring 
conventional manual input.

Machine Learning for EOG Classification 
A range of supervised classifiers has been applied to EOG 
signals. Hernández Pérez et al. [2023] evaluated EOG movement 
classification using wavelet-derived features and algorithms 
including K-nearest neighbors, Support Vector Machines, and 
decision trees. 
The present study uses three conventional classifiers: Random 
Forest, Gradient Boosting, and an RBF Support Vector Machine. 
Random Forest combines multiple randomized decision trees and 
aggregates their predictions [Breiman, 2001]. It can represent 
nonlinear

interactions

engineered signal features. 
Gradient Boosting constructs a sequence of weak predictive 
models in which later models attempt to reduce errors made by 
the existing ensemble [Friedman, 2001]. 
Support Vector Machines construct decision boundaries that 
maximize class separation in an appropriate feature space. Kernel 
functions allow nonlinear class boundaries to be represented 
without explicitly constructing the full transformed feature space 
[Cortes and Vapnik, 1995]. 
 
These models were selected because they are suitable for 
moderate-dimensional structured feature vectors and can perform 
inference without the computational requirements associated with 
larger deep-learning architectures.

EOG Feature Engineering 
Different ocular actions affect multiple properties of the 
waveform. A purely amplitude-based representation can therefore 
discard potentially useful temporal or spectral information. 
The present system combines summary statistics, waveform 
derivatives, slope, zero crossings, peak characteristics, temporal 
segment means, frequency-domain energy, dominant frequency, 
and Hjorth mobility. 
Hjorth 
[1970] 
introduced 
time-domain 
descriptors 
for 
electrophysiological signals, including mobility, which relates 
variation in the derivative of a signal to variation in the original 
waveform. In this work, Hjorth mobility is used only as a 
mathematical signal descriptor and is not interpreted as a 
physiological biomarker.

These studies demonstrate that EOG interaction is feasible, but

6. Discussion 
The results provide two different views of the EOG classifier. 
The original window-level experiment produced a hold-out 
accuracy of 91.14%, while the stricter trial-level analysis 
produced a mean cross-validation accuracy of 78.75% with 
Random Forest. 
This difference is important. 
It would be tempting to report only the larger number. However, 
doing so would give an incomplete description of the system's 
generalization because the original windows overlapped by 
87.5%. 
 
For two consecutive windows, 
W1  = x[1 : 400] 
and 
W2  = x[51 : 450], 
350 samples are shared. 
If W1 enters training and W2 enters testing, the test example 
contains much of the same underlying   physiological recording 
as the training example. 
The reconstructed trial-level experiment removes this particular 
form of overlap between evaluation examples. Its lower accuracy 
is therefore a more conservative and scientifically useful 
indication of how the classifier performs on complete recorded 
trials not duplicated through overlapping windows. 
The model-ranking difference is also notable. Gradient Boosting 
was strongest in the original analysis, whereas Random Forest 
was strongest at the trial level. The objective of this work is not to 
argue that Random Forest is universally superior for EOG.

trials not duplicated through overlapping windows.

Instead, the result demonstrates that classifier ranking can depend

Neutral trials were identified with 90% recall, and blink trials

preprocessing, or the feature representation. Such explanations 
should 
therefore 
be 
considered 
hypotheses 
rather 
than 
conclusions.

regarding the representation. Statistical features alone produced 
76.25% accuracy and frequency-domain features 75.63%, while 
the full feature vector reached 78.75%. The difference is not 
sufficiently large to claim that the 28-feature design is optimal, 
but 
it 
indicates 
that 
combining 
heterogeneous 
signal 
characteristics is at least beneficial for this dataset. 
The real-time architecture also illustrates that classification 
accuracy alone is not equivalent to interaction quality. 
An interface may have reasonable average classification accuracy

trigger actions. For this reason, the implementation uses a 
probability threshold, majority voting over four predictions, and 
an action cooldown.

additional responsiveness constraints. Since actual end-to-end

are made.

viewed as a low-cost prototype and experimental platform rather

classes, participant populations, tasks, and evaluation protocols 
prevent meaningful comparison of headline accuracy values 
alone.

9. Conclusion 
This paper presented the design and evaluation of a low-cost 
EOG-based human–computer interaction system for recognizing 
neutral gaze, upward movement, downward movement, and 
blinking. 
Vertical EOG signals were acquired using a BioAmp EXG Pill 
and ESP32 microcontroller at a configured sampling rate of 500 
Hz. The available dataset contains 64,000 samples organized into 
160 balanced trials, with 40 trials per class. 
Each trial was represented using 28 handcrafted features covering 
statistical amplitude characteristics, temporal trends, peak 
structure, frequency-domain information, and Hjorth mobility. 
The original project pipeline reported 89.27% cross-validation 
accuracy and 91.14% window-level hold-out accuracy using 
Gradient Boosting. Because the original windows overlapped by 
87.5%, the present work additionally reconstructed the underlying 
acquisition trials and performed trial-level evaluation. 
Under five-fold stratified trial-level cross-validation, Random 
Forest achieved the highest mean accuracy: 
78.75% ± 10.90% 
with mean macro F1: 
78.68% ± 10.80% 
The trial-level analysis showed particularly strong recognition of 
neutral gaze and blinking, while upward and downward 
movements were more frequently confused. 
Feature-group analysis produced its highest accuracy when all 28 
features were used, although statistical and frequency-domain 
subsets 
independently 
retained 
substantial 
discriminatory 
information. 
The classification system was also incorporated into a real-time 
interaction pipeline. Accepted upward and downward predictions 
control vertical cursor motion, while two detected blinks within 
700 ms trigger a mouse click. Confidence filtering, four-
prediction temporal voting, and a 250 ms action cooldown 
provide additional command stabilization. 
The work demonstrates that a relatively inexpensive EOG 
acquisition setup can support a functioning machine-learning-
based interaction prototype. More importantly, the comparison 
between 
overlapping- 
window 
and 
trial-level 
evaluation 
demonstrates the effect that experimental methodology can have 
on apparent classifier performance. 
The current evidence should therefore be viewed as a preliminary 
single-dataset evaluation rather than proof of subject-independent 
assistive performance. A multi-participant dataset with explicit 
participant and trial identifiers, consistent causal preprocessing, 
subject-independent validation, and quantitative interaction 
testing is required before stronger claims regarding generalization 
and usability can be made.
